item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
SCP-840 is a type of amoeba that thrives in dark, damp environments

Me: "Oh god, oh god, there are a lot of dark and damp environments in the human body…!"

Pipes and drainage systems are the preferred habitat of SCP-840. To date, there has only been one observed instance of SCP-840 colonising a natural environment (see incident report I-840A-1).

Me: "Oh, okay, so it's happened, but only rarely; creep factor going down."

The first known instance of SCP-840 colonising a natural environment was observed in ██████████, Australia. The colony was discovered by a group of four cavers, investigating an unexplored section of █████████ Caves in ████████. In an interview the cavers stated that the colony was discovered as one member of the group attempted to crawl through a narrow passageway

Me: "…What?"

Bottom line: Throughout the entire article, I was expecting something similar to those nematode things that live in holes or enclosures and suck things in - small creatures that normally inhabit non-organic areas, but are capable of taking up residence in the bodies of living animals/humans. In hindsight, it makes more sense the way it is, given that SCP-840 uses its environment as an "exoskeleton", and it also makes it a bit less cliché, so I'm still upvoting; however, the expectation of an extra horror factor carrying me through the article and then not being met at the end left me feeling kind of let down. Having it explicitly stated from the start that these things never colonize organic structures would have spared me the expectation and disappointment that almost made me give it a neutral vote before I really thought about it. Just an observation.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I like it. +1. A few minor issues:

large colonies consisting of many thousands or millions of individuals

Scale problem: that's nowhere near enough of them. Cells are tiny. Try billions. (There are several trillion cells in the human body, for reference.)

These fused colonies are capable of replicating many of the functions of organic tissues, particularly that of vital organs.

You might want to specify that you mean animal tissues and organs.

Using the exterior of the pipe as an exoskeleton SCP-840 will, over time, convert these in to an extended digestive system

The pronoun in bold is dangling: what does it refer to? The pipes?

In larger drainage spaces, such as places where piping has burst (either incidentally or as a result of a build-up of SCP-840)

And now I'm envisioning the main wet-wall of some big institutional building, the pipes one by one cracking open, a dense matrix of dripping tissue quietly filling the space behind the walls… AUGH. Nice one. :D My point is that this is sufficient to conjure that image: you could leave out some of the more explicit detail later in the article, and still cause plenty of ceramics excretion.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I don't think that every SCP needs to be dangerous so long as it's interesting, and I had never intended for this to be dangerous, but I do agree that this article is a bit lacklustre, so it may be necessary.

I love the idea of regurgitating material, and I'll probably try to work that in if that's okay with you VAE. Having someone eaten/crushed would be easy to work in; I was doing some reasearch last night befor I saw your comment Deacon, and I was thinking something like a bird's craw would make more sense too. Another way I could make this creepier would be to up the scale a lot; maybe have a few sewer workers go to investigate a blockage, only to wander in to a gigantic stomach. One of the things I wanted to imply with this article but didn't quite get around to was that this was where dead pets (maybe even people) often ended up, as they get flushed down the toilet or as the worms burrow through the ground (better yet, combine that with regurgitation).

I'll see if I can improve this when I have some spare time.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I think something more akin to a bird's craw, where large indigestible objects (rocks, for instance) are used to crush matter until it fits better and is more easily digestible. So, for instance, your spelunker suddenly gets pulled in by peristalsis, and by the time his companions can recover him, he's had several bones broken and a few square feet of skin dissolved by the acidic mucus (which, incidentally, would need to be washed off, so one hopes there's a stream nearby or our poor spelunker is in for a world of hurt…).

OTOH, not everything the Foundation contains is scary, and this is weird enough to qualify for SCP status, IMO.

Well, I said it on the IRC.. i just love this article.
An SCP object doesn't need to be excessively dangerous, and this particular one i would say sounds rather realistic , both in writing and in concept- i mean, there is a crapton of nutrients getting flushed through sewers and just think of an organism that can exploit this…
Another potential danger asides from structural problems is peristalsis… suppose you accidentally flush something it doesn't like , and in a self-preservation instinct, it'll regurgitate a (several hundred meters multiplied by internal area of pipe) meters cubic of sewage into your house… including the digestive juices.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Pretty much agreed there, but

I'd rather these be protists than worms.

I agree that these would be better as something other than worms, but I heavily dislike the term "protists" because the extent of what unifies them as a group is that they don't belong to any other kingdoms, and they're usually pretty simple. In other words, "protist" is just an informal way of saying "none of the above". They're not consistently considered a valid way of grouping organisms. A link.

It is mildly intriguing how a group of worms could replicate the organ systems, but that's not enough to carry the article and I sincerely doubt that it was intended to. In my opinion, these could be amoebas (still "protists", but a legitimate genus that just doesn't fit into a pre-existing kingdom). Given the large amounts of, er, biomass that passes through any given plumbing system, 840 could probably construct a full digestive system, operated manually by the colony.

Alternatively, they could go man-o-war style and say "fuck you, I am an organ" and be organs, looking like the pipes just one day grew a digestive system for the hell of it, which is what I think you're going for here.

And it would just make my day if a plumber stuck his arm down the drain to see what was up and the drain ate his arm.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: It's… kind of boring. This is somewhat disgusting, but nothing more than that. These aren't really scary at all, and the only danger they pose is decreasing the stability of pipes. They won't even contaminate the water supply, because they wouldn't have anything to eat in pipes that carry purified water. These also seem really hard to contain. The Foundation can't sweep the entire piping system of the world, and some time, some plumber will run into these. Just personal preference, but I'd rather these be protists than worms.
